title: The bounded-below classical equivalence
statement:
Let $X$ be a scheme and $\Lambda$ a discrete commutative ring for which the
bounded-below derived unit $L\xrightarrow{\sim}R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*L$ of
[sk-prop-sf-comparison] holds for $L\in D^+(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$.

1. $\nu_X^*$ maps $D^+(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$ into
   $D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\Proet},\Lambda)$, and $R\nu_{X,*}$ maps
   $D^+(X_{\Proet},\Lambda)$ into $D^+(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$.
2. For every $K\in D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\Proet},\Lambda)$ the counit
   $\nu_X^*R\nu_{X,*}K\to K$ is an isomorphism.

Hence $\nu_X^*$ and $R\nu_{X,*}$ are inverse equivalences between
$D^+(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$ and $D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\Proet},\Lambda)$.

proof.text:
Put $\mathcal A=\Mod(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$ and $\mathcal B=\Mod(X_{\Proet},\Lambda_X)$, where $\Lambda_X=
u_X^*\Lambda_{X,\Et}$. Work in one enlarged universe in which the underlying site categories are small relative to the modules. By [lem-pur-ringed-site-grothendieck-abelian] these are Grothendieck abelian categories, and [lem-sfb-grothendieck-k-injective] provides K-injective resolutions. The right derived direct image can therefore be computed by these resolutions, as in [def-sfb-right-derived-functor]. Write $F=
u_X^*$ for both the underived inverse image and its termwise derived functor, and $R=R
u_{X,*}$. The adjunction $F\dashv R$ and its unit $\eta$ and counit $\varepsilon$ are the bounded-below derived adjunction named in the hypothesis; we assume $\eta_L$ is invertible for every $L\in D^+(\mathcal A)$ throughout. By [det-pe-classical-sheaves-modules], the underived $F$ is exact and its essential image is precisely the classical module sheaves. Its underived right adjoint $
u_{X,*}$ is additive and left exact: the adjunction identifies maps $T	o
u_{X,*}(\ker u)$ with maps $FT	o\operatorname{dom}u$ killed by $u$, hence with maps $T	o\ker(
u_{X,*}u)$; the same argument gives preservation of zero and finite products. Additivity also follows directly by applying direct image to the addition of module sections.

source.place: paragraph (1): coefficient categories and hypotheses for the derived functors; Stacks 07A5/03DA/03DB supply the ringed-site input

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-bounded-below], $H^q(FL)\cong F(H^qL)$ naturally in $L$, and $F$ preserves every lower cohomological bound. The module-sheaf essential image in step 1 shows that these cohomology sheaves are classical, including the zero sheaf $F(0)$; by [sk-def-pe-classical-definition], $FL\in D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(\mathcal B)$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-derived-functor-negative-vanishing] to the additive left exact functor $\nu_{X,*}:\mathcal B\to\mathcal A$, with the Grothendieck categories and resolution computation of step 1: if $H^i(K)=0$ for $i<a$, then $H^i(RK)=0$ for $i<a$. Thus $R$ takes all of $D^+(\mathcal B)$ to $D^+(\mathcal A)$, and $FR$ preserves lower cohomological bounds as well.

The termwise derived functor $F$ is triangulated and satisfies $F(M[-q])\cong F(M)[-q]$ by [lem-sf-exact-functor-derived-triangulated]. Give its right adjoint $R$ the coherent shift isomorphisms supplied by [lem-weil-pbc-adjunction-shift-compatibility-unique](iii); with these isomorphisms both the unit and counit commute with shifts. Then [lem-sf-triangulated-right-adjoint] makes $R$ triangulated with precisely these shifts. Applying $R$ and then $F$ to a distinguished triangle gives a distinguished triangle for $FR$. By [lem-weil-pbc-commshift-nattrans-triangle-morphism], the three components of $\varepsilon:FR\to\mathrm{id}$ give a morphism from this image triangle to the original triangle. This verifies the connecting-map compatibility needed below, rather than assuming that arbitrary natural transformations preserve connecting morphisms.

source.place: paragraph (3), sentence concerning the counit as a transformation of triangulated functors; Stacks 0A8D

proof.text: For a classical module sheaf $G$, [det-pe-classical-sheaves-modules] gives a module sheaf $M\in\mathcal A$ and an isomorphism $F(M)\cong G$. For any integer $q$, [lem-sf-exact-functor-derived-triangulated] identifies $G[-q]$ with $F(M[-q])$. The triangle identity for $F\dashv R$ reads $\varepsilon_{F(M[-q])}\circ F(\eta_{M[-q]})=\mathrm{id}$. Since $M[-q]\in D^+(\mathcal A)$, the assumed unit is invertible there, so $\varepsilon_{F(M[-q])}=F(\eta_{M[-q]})^{-1}$. Naturality transports this isomorphism across $F(M[-q])\cong G[-q]$. Thus the counit is invertible on every shifted classical sheaf. In particular its component on zero is invertible, by taking $M=0$.

source.place: paragraph (2), one sheaf and its shifts

proof.text: Fix a bounded classical $K$ and integers $a\leq b$ with $H^q(K)=0$ outside $[a,b]$. Put $K_q=\tau_{\leq q}K$. By [lem-weil-pbc-truncation-cohomology], $H^i(K_q)=H^i(K)$ for $i\leq q$ and is zero for $i>q$. Thus every $K_q$ is bounded below and classical, and $K_{a-1}$ has zero cohomology in all degrees. The map $0\to K_{a-1}$ is an isomorphism by [lem-weil-pbc-derived-plus-iso-on-cohomology]; naturality of the counit and step 4 imply that $\varepsilon_{K_{a-1}}$ is invertible. We induct on the integer $q$ from $a$ to $b$ to show that $\varepsilon_{K_q}$ is invertible.

source.place: paragraph (3), bounded induction: lower bound, induction claim and zero base

proof.text: For $a\leq q\leq b$, use the distinguished triangle $K_{q-1}\to K_q\to H^q(K)[-q]\to K_{q-1}[1]$ of [lem-weil-pbc-truncation-triangle]. Step 3 makes its counit components a morphism of distinguished triangles, so [lem-weil-pbc-derived-cohomology-ladder] gives a commutative ladder of long exact cohomology sequences. The first and third vertical maps are isomorphisms: the first by induction and the third by step 4 since $H^q(K)$ is classical. In the five consecutive terms $H^{i-1}(H^q(K)[-q]),H^i(K_{q-1}),H^i(K_q),H^i(H^q(K)[-q]),H^{i+1}(K_{q-1})$, all four vertical maps other than the middle one are therefore isomorphisms. By [lem-weil-pbc-five-lemma], $H^i(\varepsilon_{K_q})$ is invertible for every $i$. By [lem-weil-pbc-derived-plus-iso-on-cohomology], $\varepsilon_{K_q}$ is invertible. This proves the induction. Finally $K_b\to K$ is a cohomology isomorphism in every degree by [lem-weil-pbc-truncation-cohomology] and the upper bound on $K$, hence an isomorphism by the same detection lemma. Naturality gives invertibility of $\varepsilon_K$.

source.place: paragraph (3), bounded induction: distinguished triangle, explicit five-term ladder, and identification of the final truncation

proof.text: Now let $K\in D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(\mathcal B)$, fix $m\in\mathbf Z$, and take an integer $N\geq m$. Put $T=\tau_{\leq N}K$ and let $c:T\to K$ be its inclusion. By [lem-weil-pbc-truncation-cohomology], $T$ is bounded with classical cohomology, $H^i(c)$ is an isomorphism for every $i\leq N$, and $H^{N+1}(T)=0$. In particular $H^{N+1}(c):0\to H^{N+1}(K)$ is a monomorphism. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-derived-functor-truncation-iso] to $v=\nu_{X,*}$ and this $c$; its hypotheses are exactly the Grothendieck categories, left exactness and right-derived computation checked in steps 1 and 2. It gives that $H^m(Rc)$ is invertible. Under the natural cohomology isomorphisms of [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-bounded-below], $H^m(FRc)$ identifies with $F(H^m(Rc))$ and is therefore invertible. Also $H^m(c)$ is invertible. Step 6 gives invertibility of $\varepsilon_T$. The naturality equation $H^m(\varepsilon_K)\circ H^m(FRc)=H^m(c)\circ H^m(\varepsilon_T)$ therefore makes $H^m(\varepsilon_K)$ invertible. Since $m$ was arbitrary, [lem-weil-pbc-derived-plus-iso-on-cohomology] shows that $\varepsilon_K$ is invertible. The truncation comparison cited here is exactly the lower-bound/upper-tail argument of Stacks 05TC(2); it needs no upper bound on $K$ and no finite cohomological dimension.

source.place: paragraph (4), bounded-below complexes: fix a degree and use upper truncation; Stacks 05TC(2) for the same tail-vanishing comparison

proof.text: Step 2 gives functors $F:D^+(\mathcal A)\to D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(\mathcal B)$ and $R:D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(\mathcal B)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$. Both subcategories are full. The assumed natural isomorphism $\eta:\mathrm{id}\xrightarrow{\sim}RF$ and the natural isomorphism $\varepsilon:FR\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{id}$ established in step 7 restrict to these subcategories, with the same triangle identities. These are the required mutually inverse equivalences.
